tiktok.sourceLabel: TikTok — How the For You feed works
summaries: For You ranks videos by predicted interest
Likes, shares, comments, finishes, and skips count
Tapping the sound is a signal
TikTok does not publish a completion target
tiktok.keyChanges:
TikTok says For You gives each video a score for how likely you are to interact with it, then shows the higher scores.
Signals include videos you view, like, share, comment on, or mark Not Interested, plus follows, finishing, skipping, favoriting, time spent, and tapping the sound.
TikTok also uses how other people interact and details about the video. It does not publish a formula or a required completion percentage.
If top videos are too similar, TikTok says it swaps some out so the feed is less repetitive.
The old card’s completion percentages, test-audience sizes, and audio-volume rules are not on TikTok’s page, so they were removed.
tiktok.editingTips:
A skip and the time someone spends watching are signals. Open with the point of the clip. TikTok does not publish a required length or a first-3-seconds cutoff.
Say what the video is about in the caption and on screen, in plain words.
The soundtrack matters: tapping it is one of the signals TikTok lists.
Vertical video is what For You plays. Keep the picture clear on a phone.
tiktok.postingTips:
TikTok does not publish a best clock time or a required number of posts per day.
Use your own viewer activity instead of a generic morning, lunch, and night schedule.
A pace you can keep is more useful than a burst. TikTok does not say that posting several videos at once is a penalty or a boost.
tiktok.titleTips:
The caption is how people and the system read the topic. Put the point in the first line.
A short question or a clear promise is easier to scan than a paragraph.
TikTok does not publish a character limit for reach or a required hashtag count.
tiktok.descriptionTips:
Use a few hashtags that match the clip. Unrelated tags do not make the video clearer.
The old “3–5 hashtags” and “40–70 characters” lines were not from TikTok.
A simple ask, such as a comment or a follow, is optional. It is not a published ranking lever.

summaries: Feed, Stories, Explore, and Reels rank separately
Reels predict reshares, full watches, likes, and audio
Original reels are favored over copies
No published best hour or hashtag count
instagram.keyChanges:
Instagram says Feed, Stories, Explore, and Reels each have their own ranking. There is not one algorithm.
For Reels, the ranking explainer says the main predictions are how likely someone is to reshare it, watch it all the way through, like it, and open the audio page.
Signals include what you recently liked, saved, reshared, and commented on, your history with that account, and information about the reel and the person who posted it.
Instagram’s creator guidance says a reel is first shown to a small group that may like it, including people who do not follow you, then to a wider group if they engage.
Copies and aggregator accounts are held back from recommendations. Instagram does not publish a completion-rate percentage.
instagram.editingTips:
Reels are vertical. A full watch is one of the published predictions, so make the point clear early. Instagram does not publish a required length.
On-screen words help people watching with the sound off.
Audio should fit the clip. Opening the audio page is a published signal.
Skip another app’s watermark. Instagram’s recommendation notes call out visible watermarks.
Reels longer than 3 minutes are allowed. That is a length limit, not a ranking target.
instagram.postingTips:
Instagram does not publish a universal best hour. Use Insights for when your own audience is in the app.
The old “post at 11 AM” and “3–5 Reels a week” lines were not from Instagram.
A steady pace you can keep beats a burst you cannot. Instagram has not published a penalty for posting more than once a day.
instagram.titleTips:
The first line of the caption is what people see before “more”. Say the point in plain words.
A question can invite a comment. Comments are a signal on Feed and Explore. Instagram does not publish a word-count target.
The cover or first frame should match the caption. Do not promise a different video.
instagram.descriptionTips:
Instagram’s ranking explainer does not set a hashtag count. The old “5–10 hashtags” line is not a rule.
Use a few tags that match the post.
Saves and shares are important Explore signals in the published explainer. Ask for one only when the post is actually worth keeping.

summaries: Shorts can be up to 3 minutes
Satisfaction matters, not just watch time
Original Shorts are preferred over reuploads
Interest can carry between Shorts and long videos
youtube-shorts.keyChanges:
YouTube says recommendations learn from watch history, search history, subscriptions, likes, dislikes, “Not interested”, “Don’t recommend channel”, and satisfaction surveys. There is no published recipe.
The Shorts feed is personalized to what YouTube thinks you want next. Someone who watches your long videos may also be shown your Shorts.
YouTube’s help says you can upload Shorts up to 3 minutes. The old “7–15 seconds” and “70% completion” targets are not YouTube rules.
On 1 Oct 2026 YouTube said it will show fewer Shorts that reupload someone else’s work without your own commentary, edit, or story.
youtube-shorts.editingTips:
Shoot vertical. YouTube describes Shorts as vertical videos up to 3 minutes. The get-started page notes a maximum upload resolution of 1080p.
Open with the point of the video. YouTube has not published a first-3-seconds cutoff or a required cut rate.
If you use someone else’s clip, add your own voice, edit, or story. A plain reupload is what the Oct 2026 update pushes down.
Captions help viewers. They are not described as a percentage boost.
youtube-shorts.postingTips:
YouTube does not publish a best clock time or a required number of Shorts per day. The old “1–3 a day” line was not from YouTube.
In YouTube Analytics, “When your viewers are on YouTube” is the report for your own audience.
A schedule you can keep helps people know when to come back. YouTube has not published a penalty for posting less often.
youtube-shorts.titleTips:
Say what the Short is, in words a person would search. YouTube does not publish a 3-to-5-word limit.
The title and thumbnail should match the video. A click that disappoints is something satisfaction surveys can catch.
YouTube classifies a Short from the video itself. Do not rely on a hashtag to change the ranking.
youtube-shorts.descriptionTips:
Use the description to add the topic in plain words and, if you have one, a link to a related long video.
YouTube says interest can carry across Shorts and long videos. It does not say a link is a ranking boost.
A few relevant hashtags are enough. YouTube does not publish a required count.

summaries: Homepage leans on what someone already watched
Up Next leans on the video playing now
Surveys check if a video was worth the time
No published retention or click-rate target
youtube-long.keyChanges:
YouTube’s recommendation help lists watch history, search history, subscriptions, likes, dislikes, “Not interested”, “Don’t recommend channel”, and satisfaction surveys.
The homepage mainly uses watch history. Up Next mainly uses the video that is playing.
Satisfaction surveys tell YouTube whether a video was worth the time, not only how long it played.
The old “40–50% retention” and “5–10% click rate” lines are not published thresholds.
youtube-long.editingTips:
Start with what the video will deliver. YouTube has not published a required intro length.
Clear audio and a picture people can follow matter more than a fixed cut every few seconds. That cut rate was not from YouTube.
Chapters help people skip on longer videos. YouTube documents them as a viewer control, not as a score.
There is no published ideal length of 8–15 minutes.
youtube-long.postingTips:
Pick a cadence you can keep. YouTube does not publish “1–2 videos a week” as a rule.
Use your audience’s own activity report instead of a generic weekday afternoon.
Scheduling can help you stay consistent. Scheduling itself is not described as a ranking boost.
youtube-long.titleTips:
Put the topic in the title in words people search, where a phone will not cut them off.
The thumbnail and title should match. YouTube names clicks as a signal, and surveys catch videos that disappoint after the click.
YouTube does not publish a 50–60 character rule.
youtube-long.descriptionTips:
The first lines should summarize the video, because that is what shows before “more”.
Add chapters on longer videos, useful links, and a few specific hashtags. YouTube does not publish a hashtag count.
Repeating keywords is not a documented way to get recommended.

summaries: Feed predicts comments, shares, and time well spent
Surveys ask if a post was worth your time
Reels are scored for what you are likely to enjoy
No published completion percentage
facebook-reels.keyChanges:
Meta says Feed looks at thousands of signals, including likes, shares, comments, friends, and Groups, then predicts which posts you will find relevant.
Those predictions include how likely you are to comment, how likely friends are to comment if you share, and whether a post starts a conversation. Surveys ask if a post was “worth your time”.
Problematic content can be shown less. Meta does not publish a formula or a completion cutoff.
For Reels, Meta says the system looks at signals such as length, similarity to other reels, and how well a reel matches what you interact with, then ranks a short list by a relevance score.
The old “80% completion” and “shown to 5–10% of followers” lines are not on Meta’s pages.
facebook-reels.editingTips:
Reels are vertical. Meta lists length as one signal and does not publish a required 15–30 second range.
Make the subject obvious early. Meta does not publish a first-3-seconds rule.
On-screen text helps people watching without sound. That is practical advice, not a published score.
Post the video on Facebook. Meta’s Reels page does not give a watermark penalty, so this card does not claim one.
facebook-reels.postingTips:
Meta does not publish a best clock time or a required number of Reels per week.
The old “3–5 a week” and “10 AM–1 PM” lines were removed.
Use your Page insights for when your own audience is online.
Reply to comments when you can. Feed predictions include conversation, but Meta does not say a reply multiplies reach by a set amount.
facebook-reels.titleTips:
The first line of the caption is what people see. Say the point in a few words.
A question can start the comments Meta’s Feed predictions look for. It is not a guaranteed boost.
Meta does not publish a 40-character or 100–250 character caption rule.
facebook-reels.descriptionTips:
Use a few tags that match the reel. Meta’s ranking pages do not set a hashtag count.
One clear next step is easier to understand than several asks.
Meta does not say that a keyword in the first 100 characters changes the score.

x.sourceLabel: X Help — For You home timeline
summaries: For You mixes follows and recommendations
Ranked from likes, reposts, and replies
Who you follow changes what is gathered
The help page does not publish point values
x.keyChanges:
X says For You includes posts from accounts and Topics you follow, plus recommended posts from accounts you do not follow.
After it gathers posts, X ranks them with a model trained on your interactions. It names Likes, Reposts, and Replies as examples.
Other signals it lists are accounts you follow, Topics you follow, posts you like, posts liked by people in your network, and accounts those people follow.
X says it filters harmful, abusive, or spammy content before showing posts.
The help page does not publish point values. Unofficial write-ups of source code are not used here.
x.editingTips:
A post people reply to, like, or repost matches the interactions X names. Write something a person can answer.
A photo or video can make a post clearer. X’s help page does not publish a required media size or a watch-time percentage.
Keep the first line readable. X does not publish a character target for reach.
x.postingTips:
X does not publish a best hour or a required number of posts per day.
Following accounts and Topics changes what is gathered for you, and who may see you when their network overlaps yours.
Posting when your readers are awake is common sense. It is not an official window.
x.titleTips:
The first line is the whole post for many readers. Lead with the point.
A specific claim or question invites a reply, which is one of the interactions X names.
Do not bait replies. X says it filters spam before display.
x.descriptionTips:
Hashtags and Topics help X connect a post to a subject. The help page does not set a hashtag count.
Add a link when the post needs one. X does not publish a penalty for links.
Replies you write on other posts are public interactions. They are not a documented growth trick.

summaries: People arrive from Browse, Search, and the homepage
Tags and categories are how Browse filters
Go-live notices bring followers back
Twitch does not publish a rank formula
twitch.keyChanges:
Twitch’s discovery analytics list how viewers arrive: Browse, Search, homepage recommendations, go-live notifications, other channels, and sources outside Twitch.
Tags and categories are filters on Browse and Search. Twitch shows which tags led to views and impressions. It does not publish a score called “the algorithm”.
Homepage recommendations are a listed source, separate from the homepage carousel. Twitch does not publish the signals inside that shelf.
A live stream is not a short video, so there is no official completion rate.
twitch.editingTips:
The title, category, and tags are what Browse and Search show before a click. Set them to what you are actually doing.
A clear offline picture helps the panel people see in Browse. That is presentation, not a published boost.
Clips can point people to the live channel. Twitch does not say a clip count raises live rank.
twitch.postingTips:
Go live on a rhythm your regulars can remember. Twitch lists go-live notifications as a way followers find you.
Stream when your own viewers are free. Twitch does not publish a global best hour.
Changing category mid-stream changes which Browse shelf you are on. Pick the closest true category.
twitch.titleTips:
Say the game or topic in the title in plain words. People scanning Browse need to see it.
Do not stuff the title with unrelated words. Tags have their own field, and Twitch measures those impressions separately.
A short, specific title is easier to read on a phone. Twitch does not publish a character limit for reach.
twitch.descriptionTips:
The about panel and schedule tell people when to come back. Twitch does not describe them as a ranking input.
Use tags for the real content. Custom tags are measured in discovery analytics.
Links to other sites help off-Twitch discovery, which Twitch lists as its own source. They do not replace the category.

summaries: Recommendations follow what people watch
Home has a carousel, For You, and categories
A stream in the last 7 days is more likely
No published viewer-count target
kick.keyChanges:
Kick says recommendations use your viewing activity and patterns across the community. The more someone uses Kick, the more the suggestions narrow.
Kick names four places: the home carousel (your activity plus streams the Kick team picks), Streams For You, Categories For You, and Recommended channels in the side list.
For streamers, Kick says it favors channels whose viewership and watch time are growing week to week, channels that streamed at least once in the past seven days, and new channels that streamed at least once in the past three days.
A more recent stream is more likely to be recommended. Kick does not publish a follower cutoff or a required average-viewer number.
kick.editingTips:
The title and category tell people, and the homepage, what the stream is. Set them to the real topic.
The offline header is the short strip people see when you are not live. Keep words near the center, because the tall file is cropped to that strip. That is layout, not a ranking rule.
Clips can be browsed from the homepage. Kick does not say a clip style raises live recommendations.
kick.postingTips:
Kick says channels that streamed more recently are more likely to be recommended, and it calls out the past seven days, or three days for a new channel.
A long gap makes a recommendation less likely. There is no published best clock time.
The Following page is how regulars find you. Recommendations are the extra shelf for people who do not follow you yet.
kick.titleTips:
Use the category people would browse, plus a plain title. Kick groups streams by category.
Do not promise a game or topic you are not streaming.
Kick does not publish a title length for reach.
kick.descriptionTips:
The about section and social links help someone decide to follow. Kick does not describe them as ranking signals.
The recommender article does not give a tag count. Use the category first.
Week-to-week watch time is the outcome Kick says it looks for, not a caption trick.
